goals: Model curved relationships with polynomial terms
why: Many relationships curve: fuel use vs speed, yield vs fertiliser, sales vs price. Polynomial terms let a linear model bend while staying simple and interpretable.
explain: Add new features x², x³ … and fit an ordinary linear regression on them. The model is still "linear in the coefficients", so the same least-squares machinery works.
Degree 2 gives one bend (a U or an inverted U); degree 3 gives two bends.
High degrees overfit dramatically: a degree-15 polynomial threads through every training point and swings wildly in between and at the edges.
Choose the degree by cross-validation, scale the features first, and consider splines as a smoother alternative.

example.title: Finding the most economical speed
steps: Straight line: fuel = 6.3 + 0.004 × speed, R² ≈ 0.02: it says speed hardly matters
Degree 2 fit: fuel ≈ 13.5 − 0.2017 × speed + 0.001286 × speed², R² ≈ 0.9997; b₂ > 0, so the curve is a U
Best speed = 0.2017 / (2 × 0.001286) ≈ 78.4 km/h, using about 5.59 litres per 100 km
example.result: The quadratic captures the "sweet spot" speed (cruise at about 75 to 80 km/h), which no straight line can.

mistakes: Picking a high degree because the training R² is higher.
Extrapolating a polynomial (it explodes outside the data range).
takeaways: Add powers of x to model curves
use: Smooth curved relationships with a known shape (one peak or trough)
avoid: Many features (the number of terms explodes): use trees or GAMs

practice.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
v = np.array([40, 60, 80, 100, 120]).reshape(-1, 1); L = np.array([7.5, 6.0, 5.6, 6.2, 7.8])
m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(2), LinearRegression()).fit(v, L)
print(m.predict([[70], [90]]).round(2))   # [5.68 5.76]

options: It is linear in the coefficients
check.why: The model is a weighted sum of (transformed) features.

check.q: Training R² rises from degree 3 to 12, but CV error rises too. Choose…
options: Degree 3 (or whichever has the lowest CV error)
check.why: Choose by validation error, not training fit.

formula.tex: \hat y = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 x^2 + \dots + b_d x^d, \qquad x^{*} = -\frac{b_1}{2\,b_2}
formula.plain: A starting value plus weights on x, x², … up to x to the power d, fitted by least squares. For a quadratic, the turning point is at minus b₁ over twice b₂.
